extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral and political philosophy (Aristotelian ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting normative criteria and evaluative standards Aristotle sets out for different kinds of friendship, their causes, durability, duties between friends and relatives, and how justice/proportion governs reciprocal relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three kinds of friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships are of three kinds: those based on goodness (virtue), those based on pleasure, and those based on utility (advantage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle repeatedly distinguishes these categories and treats them as the primary typology for analyzing friendship. Use this classification to diagnose motivations and likely durability of particular friendships: virtue-based friendships are independent and disinterested, pleasure- and utility-based friendships depend on changing circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality vs inequality in friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Friends may be on a footing of equality or in relations of superiority and inferiority; those who are equal should be equalised in the friendship, and unequal friends should render friendship in proportion to their relative positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When parties are unequal, justice requires proportionate reciprocation (not necessarily identical returns). Practical guidance: superior persons should receive greater respect; needy persons should receive greater material aid or profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionate justice preserves friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion is the measure that equalises and preserves friendship: where exchange is proportionate, friendships are maintained; where distribution is contrary to right proportion, friendships (and political constitutions) decay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in market relations a common monetary measure preserves exchange (cobbler/weaver); in political life, misproportion leads to oligarchy etc. Apply the proportionality principle when judging fairness of returns between friends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability depends on the motive of friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships based on moral character (goodness) are permanent; those based on pleasure or advantage are liable to dissolve when pleasure or advantage ceases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use motive as predictor of longevity: virtue-based friendships are independent and disinterested and therefore stable; pleasure/utility friendships are contingent and more easily broken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of discharging debts/obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The requital of benefits (discharging an existing debt) is generally a higher duty than unsolicited kindness to companions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cases of conflicting duties, repaying a benefactor or fulfilling an existing obligation typically has higher moral weight than giving new favors. Examples include ransom situations and repayable loans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for measuring a kindness (who determines value)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a dispute whether to measure a kindness by the good conferred on the receiver or by the kind intention of the giver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's applied rule: in friendships based on utility, the advantage to the receiver is the relevant standard; in virtue-based friendships the motive (goodwill) of the doer is the proper measure. Where the original dealing was explicitly for return, the requital should be proportionate and agreed upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal (specified) versus moral (unspecified) friendships
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships of advantage may be legal (specified quid pro quo) or moral (unspecified expectations); legal obligations are clearer and admit of less dispute than moral ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal-kind friendships are enforceable and have defined terms; moral-kind friendships rely on mutual understanding and forbearance (e.g., delayed repayment). Some legal systems refuse actions on voluntary dealings to preserve trust/spirit of the arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to dissolve a friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: It is permissible to end friendships of pleasure or utility when the motivating qualities cease; in virtue-based friendships one has a right to complain if the other pretends to have goodness when they do not; a friendship should be broken when the friend is incurably depraved, though one should attempt reform where amendment is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the original ground of friendship still exists. If deceit about motives occurred, the deceived party may justly take offense. If only one party morally improves greatly, some residual obligations of past intimacy permit leniency but full mutual friendship may be impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deception about grounds of friendship is a grave wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: When someone pretends to be a friend for reasons other than they claim (e.g., feigning virtue when they are mercenary), the deceived party has just cause for stronger complaint—comparable to receiving false coin—because the object is more precious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an anti-pattern: friendships founded on false representation of motives are morally defective and justify severance or complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friends are 'another self'—definition of friend
rubrics_metrics.description: A friend is one who intends and does what is good (or what he believes to be good) to another for that other's sake; alternatively, one who lives with another and chooses the same objects or sympathises in joys and sorrows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a normative test: a true friend acts for the other's sake (not for benefit or mere pleasure) and shares final goods; the analogy to self-friendship helps evaluate depth of mutual concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship grounded on common origin and shared life
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships of kindred and companions arise from community of origin, upbringing, nearness of age and shared life—these factors strengthen friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Families, brothers raised together, and companions of the same age are likely to have the strongest opportunities for proving and trusting one another; degree of kinship and proximity of upbringing modulate bond strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political constitutions mirror domestic friendship relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Different forms of constitution (kingship, despotism, aristocracy, oligarchy, timocracy, democracy) have corresponding types of friendship; extent of friendship and justice varies with regime (e.g., kingship paternal, despotism lacks friendship).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use political analogy: where rulers seek common good (king), friendships and justice flourish; where rulers seek self-advantage (despot), friendship and justice are scant. This criterion ties individual friendships to broader civic justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fault-finding common in advantage-based friendships
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships motivated by utility are especially liable to complaint and contention because expectations and requirements tend to expand and recipients may feel under-recompensed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize this predictable failure mode: expanding demands and mismatched expectations often break utility friendships; legalizing the terms or clarifying expectations can mitigate disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who should set the value when no stipulation exists
rubrics_metrics.description: In dealings without pre-agreed terms, Aristotle observes the receiver often fixes the value; historically (Protagoras) the learner estimates the worth of knowledge he received and pays accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: where no stipulation exists, fairness may permit the receiver to set the value (especially when the receiver is the first beneficiary). A separate maxim: 'With specified reward a friend should be content.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Teachers/learners and non-monetary goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophic instruction cannot be exactly priced; where value is non-monetary (e.g., knowledge), parties should do what they can, and requital should be proportionate to ability—similar to duties toward gods or parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat non-monetary exchanges with charity and proportionality: perform what is possible rather than insisting on exact equivalence; avoid forcing market measures onto intrinsically non-market goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligations to parents and elders are special but bounded
rubrics_metrics.description: One ought to assist and honour parents in preference to others because of debt of origin, but parental claims are not unlimited; honours due vary by role and are not identical to honours due other kinds of superiors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide age- and role-appropriate respect (standing, yielding place, rites). Distinguish honours appropriate to a father from those due to a scientist or general; practical prioritization: maintenance and certain honours to parents rank highly but are contextual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Past intimacy creates residual obligations toward former friends
rubrics_metrics.description: Where friendship has ceased because of differential improvement rather than depravity, the improved party owes some allowance reflecting past intimacy (favours, leniency), though full friendship need not continue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging conduct between former friends, weigh past ties and offer reasonable forbearance where severance is not due to grave moral change.
